title: GPT4.5, QWEN TAKES DEEPSEEK's CROWN & CANCER PREDICTION: Jimmy & Matt debate their favourite AI stories from March 2025
description: Send us Fan Mail From disappointing model releases to revolutionary coding breakthroughs, our latest roundup explores the rapidly evolving AI landscape that's transforming how we work, create, and even approach medical research. We dive into the underwhelming launch of GPT-4.5, which despite Sky-high expectations and claims of improved emotional intelligence, delivered marginal improvements at twelve times the cost. Meanwhile, Alibaba quietly released Q-Wen, a coding model that matches capabilities of systems twenty times its size—and runs on a standard laptop. Does this take the crown from DeepSeek as China's top AI model? The democratization of AI continues with tools like Cursor, which paired with Claude 3.7 can build entire functioning websites from simple descriptions in minutes, radically changing what's possible for non-developers. While video generation tools like Sora finally reach European shores, we question whether current implementations truly solve meaningful problems or just create novelty. The most promising developments may be happening in medicine, where AI systems predict cancer years in advance and accelerate research cycles from months to days. Yet all this progress comes against a shifting regulatory backdrop, with the EU implementing its first AI Act provisions while global discourse pivots troublingly from "safety" to "security." As one expert notes: "AI companies don't care if you become dependent and manipulable"—highlighting why proper governance frameworks must keep pace with technological advancement. Join us as we separate the hype from reality and explore what these developments mean for our collective future.
summary: The March 2025 roundup opens with Matt gleefully slagging off GPT-4.5 (12x the API price, no point to it, 'Sam Altman is a dick') and Jimmy marveling at Alibaba's 32-billion-parameter Qwen coder matching DeepSeek's 600-billion model on a laptop. The hosts test agentic AI live (Cursor in yolo mode builds a satirical website mid-recording), shrug at video generation, celebrate quiet medical breakthroughs - MIT's Sybil predicting lung cancer six years early - and mourn the collapse of the AI safety narrative from Paris to California.
keyTalkingPoints: GPT-4.5: 12x the API cost of 4o for marginal gains; OpenAI's model lineup (o1, o3 mini, 4.5, 4.1) is an incoherent 'which cheese do you want' mess
Qwen2.5-Coder: 32bn parameters, 1/20th of DeepSeek's size, runs on a gaming laptop, matches frontier coding models - open weight on Hugging Face

Manus: the first semi-useful autonomous agent (Chinese, invite-only) - Matt won't grant a beta Chinese company autonomy over his computer; Jimmy's Cursor demo built an entire joke website about Matt mid-recording
Video generation (Sora/Veo) remains a creative disappointment - translating the image in your head into prompts is the unsolved bottleneck

Medical AI quietly winning: Google's co-scientist validated antimicrobial hypotheses; MIT Sybil predicts lung cancer 6 years out at 89% accuracy; 58 new cancer mutational signatures from 12,000 genomes

Safety in retreat: EU AI Act's first wave is live but isolated, the Paris summit dropped 'safety' from its name, and Matt channels Luiza Jarovsky: 'AI companies don't care if you become dependent and manipulable'

jimmy: Qwen's tiny coding model matching DeepSeek on consumer hardware shows open-weight progress compounding insanely fast
Cursor-class agentic coding is nuts - anyone slightly techie should try it, and model choice will soon be about speed over raw capability
Video generation won't replace the creative act - the prompt-translation bottleneck makes it a CGI-filler tool, not a creativity tool
matt: GPT-4.5 has no reason to exist; OpenAI's sprawl of overlapping models is user-hostile
The biggest near-term AI gains are medical - pattern recognition over huge datasets is exactly what AI is good at
Governance is being cast aside in a manufactured US-vs-China good-versus-evil frame; only independent governance can check big tech
